description: The figure presents three side-by-side bar charts—labeled (a) WikiText, (b) PTB, and (c) C4—comparing the perplexity performance of two quantization methods, “Uniform” (blue) and “Ours” (orange), across four different quantization bit levels: 3, 4, 8, and 16. In each chart, the horizontal axis represents the number of quantization bits, while the vertical axis measures perplexity on a linear scale ranging from 0 to 30 in (a) and (c), and 0 to 400 in (b). In (a) WikiText, the “Uniform” method achieves perplexity values of approximately 29.5 (3-bit), 27.2 (4-bit), 26.7 (8-bit), and 26.7 (16-bit), while “Ours” achieves lower values: ~21.7, ~19.0, ~18.4, and ~18.4 respectively, indicating consistent improvement. In (b) PTB, “Uniform” shows significantly higher perplexity: ~405 (3-bit), ~315 (4-bit), ~300 (8-bit), and ~300 (16-bit), while “Ours” achieves ~245, ~180, ~185, and ~185, again demonstrating superior performance. In (c) C4, “Uniform” yields perplexity values of ~28.0 (3-bit), ~25.0 (4-bit), ~24.7 (8-bit), and ~24.7 (16-bit), whereas “Ours” achieves ~20.7, ~18.2, ~17.8, and ~17.8, again showing a clear advantage. Across all datasets, the “Ours” method consistently achieves lower perplexity than “Uniform” at every bit level, with the largest relative gains observed at lower bit widths (especially 3 and 4 bits), and diminishing but still present improvements at higher bit widths. The bars are grouped by quantization bit level, with “Uniform” always positioned to the left of “Ours” within each group, and the legend is consistently placed in the top-left corner of each subplot.
